goods.barterNote: The universal measure. Every faction prices its offers against the litre. A single bottle can buy a night's silence—or a bullet.
Tier-zero scrap; the fallback value everything else is compared against. A handful can patch a hole in the bunker wall—or a hole in a man.
Shortage-spiked when supplies run thin. The white cloth turns pink before it turns red. The antiseptic stings worse than the wound.
The medicine tier anchor; the sick room's price follows it. The pills are bitter, the cure is worse than the disease. But it works.
Rises when the fallout maps update. The taste is metallic and leaves a film on the tongue. One pill a day keeps the thyroid at bay.
The generators drink it; so does the market. A full can means warmth through the night. An empty can means a long, cold watch.
Ammo holds value better than most promises. The brass is tarnished, the powder smells old. But a bullet is a bullet when the lights go out.
Tools are inelastic: scarce on supply, steady on price. The prying end is polished bright from use. It opens doors, crates, and arguments.
Storm weather moves this faster than any argument. The straps are frayed, the filter is questionable. But it's better than breathing in whatever's out there.
The registrar's pen; calibration keeps its price honest. The needle jumps like a spooked animal. That's never a good sign.
Food spikes hardest in the shortage windows. The label claims 'balanced nutrition.' The contents suggest it's been balanced with something else entirely.
Luxury softens when supplies run short — nobody trades shine for thirst. The cut diamond in a velvet box is worth more than the bunker's generator.
Cupola fuel and the ice road's payload; scarce when the window closes. The chunks are black and heavy, leaving dust on everything they touch.
Lead-antimony pipe owed to the membrane hall under the Brine Pipe Exchange. The metal is worth more than the pipe itself. The pipe is worth more than your life.
Counted by the bundle; the road charter's quota good. A handful can save a life—or end one. The ice doesn't care which.
Chilled-flange drums for the barge windlass and Berth 9. The weight is the value. The drum is the difference between a working barge and a sunken one.
The wasteland's only reliable luxury. A slab of cooked meat at the trade table makes the room go quiet. People who haven't eaten it in months will trade things they swore they would never trade.
The ceramic heart of the purifier. A bunker with a spare filter is a bunker with a future. The element is good for a season, then it trades down to the desperate at half price.
The bunker's lungs. Demand spikes with every fallout storm. The paper is three years old and brittler than the people who depend on it.
Rendered fat and wintergreen oil in a tin. It stops the black from spreading. In the deep freeze, a tin of salve is worth more than a pistol.

Sealed foil packets from the last agricultural station. Kale, potato eyes, and the beans that grow in cardboard. A single packet is the difference between a greenhouse and a cold room. Caravans that carry these are guarded like ambulances.
Acids, solvents, powders in unlabeled jars. The foundry district runs on them. Handle with care — the jars have no labels, and the smell tells you what the label would have said.
Circuit boards, wiring, chips. The gold pins still shine. Some of it is worth nothing; some of it is a radio waiting for a soldering iron. People sort it by hand, in the evenings.
Gears, shafts, bearings in a greasy bag. They rebuild pumps, generators, latches. The wasteland runs on salvage, and this is what salvage looks like before it becomes a tool.
The sun still does its part. A charged cell feeds a battery; a broken one is still the best glass around. First pick, first price, no haggling — the only utility left that hasn't failed.
A canvas kit with rolled bandages, tape, scissors and antiseptic. What a bunker calls a clinic. People who carry one walk a little straighter, and everyone notices.

Decorporation medication in foil. It pulls accumulated dose out of the body — not a cure, a deduction. Pharmacies that still stand trade it only for things they cannot scavenge. People argue over the last pack like it is a promise.

A polymer membrane sheet from the water treatment plant. It turns brine into drinking water under pressure. The flotilla settlements trade these at a premium — they are the difference between a working barge and a stranded one.

Deep-blue decorporation pellets in a sealed medical vial. They bind cesium and thallium in the gut. Pre-war pharmaceutical stock — the last production run was the year the exchange stopped everything. Each vial is a non-renewable resource.

A small lead-lined cask with a threaded lid, used for transporting hot samples. Science teams trade these like currency. The lead is the value; the shielding is the purpose. Without it, no one can study what the ground has become.

A spiral-wound RO element. The heart of the advanced water purifier. Foundry district workshops rebuild these from salvaged housing and new membrane sheets. The flotilla pays double — their stills run on these.
A twist of copper wire shaped into a loop. The cheapest passive catch a survivor can make. Breaks often, catches little, costs almost nothing. Every scavenger has set one at least once.

A wooden box with a gravity door and a treadle trigger. Dependable, reusable, and bulky. Workshop hunters build these from salvaged lumber and scrap metal. The animal lives inside it, which is either mercy or a problem.

A woven funnel of wood and cord set in moving water. Fish enter but cannot find the exit. Strong where geography supports it, worthless where it does not. The freeze kills it. The thaw brings it back.
Rifle rounds ride behind the frontline convoys; the price climbs with every skirmish report.
Shell bags trade steady at the strongholds and slow everywhere else.
Rail sidings and river barges burn it by the drum; the price follows the timetable.
Keeps for weeks without ice, so it sells wherever the next meal is uncertain.
Sealed jars of brine-cured greenhouse produce; the salt camps never run short of buyers.
Trades far above its weight wherever a garrison has been paid recently.
Encrypted warehousing codes sell to whoever has trucks and no scruples. The sheet outlives the handshake.
Nobody reads them and everybody wants them sealed. Bureaucracy is the one crop that never froze.
Garrisons pay the rack price without haggling. Sidearms hold value because nobody admits wanting one.
Two pipes and a belief in tomorrow. Sells at dusk in camps that heard something outside the wire.
Traded in whispers and wrapped in the same cloth as the bandages. The price doubles wherever the mines are working.
Still unsticks from itself, which puts it ahead of most promises. Every repair job starts and ends with it.
Ten metres of three-strand hemp. Quarries and lighthouses measure rope in lives, so they never haggle hard.
Nobody admits what's on it. Music, a sermon, somebody's last recorded voice — morale is whatever plays.
